meta.title: FROTH-RFC-0015: Sequential Cycle Items
meta.author: Charlie (@charliebuddybot)
meta.related: FROTH-RFC-0004, FROTH-RFC-0005, FROTH-RFC-0008, FROTH-RFC-0014, FROTH-RFC-0017, FROTH-RFC-0019

section.title: Problem
section.p: Froth currently models an agent transcript as a parent-linked message chain plus a separate event log that stores the latest head pointer.
In concrete terms:

item.p: agent_messages rows point to prior rows via parent_id
agent events record head_id snapshots over time
readers recover the cycle transcript by finding the latest head and then recursively walking ancestors back to the root

section.p: This was a clever representation. It is no longer a pleasant one.
The current model is confusing because it splits one obvious thing, "the ordered contents of a cycle," into several indirect pieces:

item.p: the cycle row
the latest head pointer inferred from events
the parent-linked message DAG
extra event rows that describe runtime structure separately from the semantic chain

section.p: It is also slow and awkward. Common operations such as "load this cycle transcript", "show me the last assistant item", and "render the cycle in order" all require head lookup and recursive traversal. That is exactly the wrong ergonomics for the hottest conceptual path in the subsystem.

Worse, the DAG shape suggests capabilities that Froth does not actually use well. Most cycles are experienced and inspected as a linear sequence of items. The branching structure is latent complexity without corresponding operator value.

section.title: Goal
section.p: Make cycles first-class ordered entities.
A cycle should own a sequential series of items directly, so the obvious questions have obvious answers:

item.p: What is in this cycle?
In what order?
What is the latest item?
Which item corresponds to a tool call, a tool result, a user prompt, or a final reply?

section.p: The model should optimize for the shape Froth actually uses: an ordered turn log attached to one cycle.

item.p: This RFC does not abolish agent cycles as durable run records.
This RFC does not require every token delta to be persisted as a cycle item.
This RFC does not redesign the general telemetry span system.
This RFC does not require that all runtime facts move into cycle items; some remain better represented as generic events or facts.

section.title: Thesis
section.p: Froth should scrap the parent-chased transcript DAG as the primary persistence model for cycles.

Instead, each cycle should have ordered items with stable sequence numbers. Readers should load a cycle by querying its items in sequence order, not by reconstructing a root from a head pointer and then walking ancestry.
The key simplification is:

item.p: current model: cycle -> latest head event -> head message -> recursive parent walk
proposed model: cycle -> ordered items

section.p: That is both easier for humans to understand and easier for code to query correctly.

subsection.title: 1. Introduce `cycle_items` as the primary transcript structure
subsection.p: Add a table that belongs directly to a cycle and is ordered by sequence.
One plausible shape is:
subsection.code: cycle_items id ulid/uuid NOT NULL primary key cycle_id ulid/uuid NOT NULL seq bigint NOT NULL role text NULL item_kind text NOT NULL payload jsonb NOT NULL default '{}' span_id text NULL inserted_at timestamp NOT NULL
subsection.p: At minimum, (cycle_id, seq) should be unique and indexed.
The important property is that the cycle's semantic log is now attached to the cycle explicitly rather than inferred through a message ancestry structure.

subsection.title: 2. Items are ordered facts, not parent-linked nodes
subsection.p: A cycle item does not need a transcript parent_id.
Ordering comes from seq. Identity comes from id. Membership comes from cycle_id.
This means the fundamental query becomes simple:
No recursive CTE is needed to read the cycle in order. No latest-head lookup is needed first. No extra dance is required to discover what the last item was.

subsection.p: Examples of useful item_kind values:

Some deployments may prefer a smaller surface where role and payload carry more meaning. That is fine. The main requirement is that the item row itself tells readers what species of thing it is without joining through a head event.

subsection.title: 4. `agent_cycles` should carry direct summary pointers, not indirect head inference
subsection.p: If Froth wants summary fields for speed, they should live directly on agent_cycles or a projection table.
Examples:
Those are normal projections over the ordered items. They are clearer than "look through events to find the last head_id that happens to point into a parent-linked chain."

subsection.title: 5. Keep runtime events, but stop making them own the transcript
subsection.p: Execution events are still useful for runtime inspection. They can keep recording:

item.p: cycle started/completed/failed
LLM requests
tool starts and finishes
timeouts and errors

subsection.p: But they should no longer serve as the authoritative location of the transcript head.
That split is cleaner:

item.p: cycle_items = ordered semantic contents of the cycle
events or other fact streams = operational record of what happened while producing those items

subsection.title: 6. Branching should be explicit and rare, not the default transcript model
subsection.p: If Froth later needs true branching or alternative continuations, that should be modeled explicitly rather than hidden inside the default transcript structure.
For example:

item.p: a separate link relation between cycle items
a derived_from edge for resumed or forked runs
a new cycle spawned from an earlier item

subsection.p: Branching is not forbidden. It is simply no longer the base mental model for ordinary cycle storage.

subsection.title: Operator Clarity
subsection.p: Humans think of a cycle as a sequence. The storage model should agree.
The proposed model removes several recurring sources of confusion:

item.p: no separate "root entity" hunt through a parent chain
no need to explain why the cycle transcript is not directly on the cycle
no special conceptual role for "head" as the gateway to reading the cycle

subsection.title: Query Simplicity
subsection.p: Hot queries become trivial:

item.p: load cycle transcript
load last N items
find final assistant reply
render the cycle in the UI

subsection.p: These all become straightforward indexed queries over cycle_id and seq.

subsection.title: Performance
subsection.p: Recursive traversal is not free, especially when it sits on the hot path of inspection tools and UI rendering.
A sequential table gives Froth the storage pattern it actually wants:

item.p: append-heavy writes
ordered reads by cycle
cheap access to the tail of the cycle

section.title: Migration Strategy

item.p: Stop the full Froth node so there are no concurrent transcript writes during the cutover.
Introduce cycle_items and reconstruct the existing ordered history from retained agent events and their blob-backed full payloads.
Update writers and readers such as workers, transcript tools, follow views, and cycle inspectors to use cycle_items.
Stop treating head_id in events as the authoritative transcript pointer and remove the recursive read path.
Keep the former message table as a non-runtime archive where it still exists; do not retain a dual-write or compatibility path.

section.p: This is an offline, direct migration rather than an incremental dual-write. Once the node restarts, the cycle owns its ordered items directly and there is only one active transcript representation.

item.p: Cycle storage matches the mental model operators and readers already use.
Transcript readers become much simpler and faster.
The head-pointer plus recursive-parent machinery stops being a central dependency.
Branching becomes an explicit advanced feature instead of ambient complexity.
This introduces a new primary transcript table and requires an offline data migration.
Some existing code paths that currently assume Message rows and head_id pointers will need to be rewritten.
If true in-cycle branching ever becomes a first-class need, it will need an explicit representation rather than piggybacking on parent pointers.

section.title: Recommendation
section.p: Froth should stop modeling the primary contents of a cycle as a parent-linked DAG that must be reconstructed from a head pointer.

Make cycles into direct ordered entities with sequential items. Keep runtime events for operational truth, but let transcript inspection be a simple ordered read instead of a recursive recovery procedure.

section.title: Relationship to RFC-0017
section.p: RFC-0017 proposes a much broader replacement for Froth's system-wide persistence ontology. It does not supersede this focused simplification of the agent runtime that exists today.

The cycle_items table is the direct transcript representation for the current architecture. If Froth later adopts the ontological core, that implementation may absorb cycle items or expose the same ordered interface as a projection. That possible future migration is not a reason to retain the current parent-linked transcript machinery.

section.title: Implementation Status
section.p: Implemented on 2026-07-25 as a direct, offline cutover.

The implementation adds and populates cycle_items, moves runtime writers and readers to ordered cycle queries, and removes agent_messages, head pointers, recursive transcript reads, and storage compatibility fallbacks from the runtime. Existing transcript history is reconstructed into the new canonical representation from retained agent events and blob-backed payloads; the former message table is retained as an unused archive on databases where it still exists.

For cycles older than the canonical agent-event payloads, the data migration also recovers exact user-visible Telegram inputs and outputs where a durable cycle link still identifies them. Those fallback items carry explicit recovery provenance and do not claim to reproduce unavailable internal prompt context or tool traces.
